newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Migration to Russia slowed in 1996, official says.
newsitem.headline: Migration to Russia slowed in 1996, official says.

text.p: The flow of ethnic Russian immigrants from former Soviet republics into Russia fell in 1996 as economic hardship reduced the lure of the homeland, the country's top immigration official said on Wednesday.
But independent analysts questioned the figures, suggesting many new arrivals, seeing no hope of official help to find a home, were failing to register with the authorities.

Tatyana Regent, head of the Federal Migration Service, said about 700,000 migrants from other former Soviet Republics registered as moving to Russia in 1996, down from 1.1 million in 1994 and 960,000 last year.

"The main reason for the decline is the worsening economic situation in Russia," she told reporters. "Earlier people came with the hope that things would be better in the traditional centre for Russians."

The 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union splintered the empire into 15 countries, leaving millions of Russians in Ukraine, stranding others in the Baltic states and Central Asia, and dividing families across new national borders.
For many ethnic Russians now a minority in new countries the path to Russia seemed natural. War in the Central Asian nation of Tajikistan also drove out thousands, including non-Russians.

In Moscow, politicians such as ultranationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky made the plight of their ethnic kin abroad a burning issue. Zhirinovsky paints an apocalyptic picture of Russian women abused and families intimidated and hounded out of their homes by local nationalists.

The reality bears no resemblance to this, though there have certainly been many instances of intimidation. Russians have also felt alienated as Russian language and culture have lost their privileged position.
The first wave of arrivals in Russia easily obtained "forced migrant" or refugee status entitling them to Russian government help. But those funds have now run short.

"In 1996, it's much more difficult I understand, for people to get registered as 'forced migrants'," said James Bissett, head of the Moscow office of the Swiss-based International Organisation for Migration.
"Consequently, a lot of people might come back who don't get registered," he said. "In actual fact, the numbers coming may be even, if anything, increasing."

Zhanna Zayonchkovskaya, an assistant director at the Academy of Sciences' Institute of Economic Forecasts, said the real number of immigrants is at least 50 percent higher than the official statistics.

At the news conference, Regent acknowledged that the Federal Migration Service was unable to help many of the new arrivals with housing and other pressing needs because of poor financing. She said for example that 240,000 new arrivals were waiting for housing at the end of 1996.
The transition is difficult for many of the new arrivals as they are usually forced to settle in rural areas in southern Russia and Siberia as larger cities often require special residence permits.

"The people are suffering a lot of hardship, they are really scrambling," Bissett said. "Some of them are living in old box cars, others are lucky enough to get a locality in which the local government will help them a little."
